    91|## 2. How Generated Data Gets Into Snowflake
    92|
    93|The `riskcopilot generate` command takes raw academic data (AMLworld HI-Small -- 5 million
    94|financial transactions with known money laundering labels) and transforms it into realistic
    95|Indian banking data:
    96|
    97|- Names become Indian names (en_IN Faker): "Rajesh Kumar", "Sunita Devi"
    98|- Amounts are in INR with realistic distributions
    99|- Channels are Indian payment rails: RTGS, NEFT, SWIFT, UPI
   100|- Branches are in Delhi, Mumbai, Pune
   101|- 10 parties have planted structuring patterns (cash deposits just below Rs 10 lakh)
   102|- One "hero" party triggers every detection rule (for demo purposes)
   103|
   104|The output is Parquet files with a SHA-256 manifest (byte-identical per seed -- the same
   105|seed always produces the same data).
   106|
   107|The `riskcopilot load` command then does a single-transaction load into Snowflake:
   108|
   109|```
   110|Your laptop                         Snowflake
   111|----------                          ---------
   112|parties.parquet        ----COPY---> RAW.RAW_PARTY
   113|accounts.parquet       ----COPY---> RAW.RAW_ACCOUNT
   114|transactions.parquet   ----COPY---> RAW.RAW_AMLWORLD_TRANS  (5,078,345 rows)
   115|relationships.parquet  ----COPY---> RAW.RAW_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP
   116|profiles.parquet       ----COPY---> RAW.RAW_DECLARED_PROFILE
   117|labels.parquet         ----COPY---> GROUND_TRUTH.GROUND_TRUTH_STAGE  (isolated)
   118|```
   119|
   120|The load runs in **one transaction** -- if any table fails, everything rolls back. After
   121|the load, the raw tables contain the full generated dataset, and everything downstream is
   122|automatic.
   123|
   124|**Why this matters for the agent:** The agent never reads RAW directly. It reads from
   125|CURATED and EVIDENCE_CHAIN, which are computed from RAW by dynamic tables. But the data
   126|the agent ultimately presents in an STR -- the transaction amounts, party names, account
   127|numbers -- all originated from this generated dataset.

   131|## 3. What Is a Dynamic Table and Why Do We Need Them?
   132|
   133|### The problem dynamic tables solve
   134|
   135|After `riskcopilot load`, you have 5 million raw transaction rows sitting in `RAW.RAW_AMLWORLD_TRANS`. Each row is a single transaction leg -- a debit or a credit. It looks like this:
   136|
   137|```
   138|txn_id       | debit_account | credit_account | amount  | timestamp           | is_cash
   139|-------------|---------------|----------------|---------|---------------------|--------
   140|TXN-00000001 | A-000000042   | A-000000099    | 950000  | 2022-09-05 10:23:00 | true
   141|TXN-00000002 | A-000000042   | A-000000101    | 980000  | 2022-09-07 14:15:00 | true
   142|TXN-00000003 | A-000000042   | A-000000101    | 970000  | 2022-09-09 09:47:00 | true
   143|... 5 million more rows ...
   144|```
   145|
   146|But to detect structuring, you don't want raw rows. You need to ask questions like:
   147|
   148|- "Which parties deposited cash into 2+ different accounts within 7 days?"
   149|- "Were those deposits between 90% and 99.9% of Rs 10 lakh?"
   150|- "What is this party's name, KYC status, and branch?"
   151|
   152|Answering these questions requires **joining** multiple tables (transactions + parties + accounts + policy clauses), **aggregating** (group by party and time window), and **filtering** (only cash deposits in the structuring band). You could write a SQL query that does all of this, but:
   153|
   154|- It would take minutes to run on 5 million rows
   155|- You'd have to run it manually every time new data arrives
   156|- The results would be stale the moment new transactions come in
   157|
   158|### What a dynamic table actually is
   159|
   160|A dynamic table is a **query result that Snowflake keeps up to date for you**. You write the query once (as a `CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE` statement), and Snowflake re-runs it automatically on a schedule you specify.
   161|
   162|Think of it like a spreadsheet formula. If cell A1 has `=SUM(B1:B100)`, you don't re-type the formula every time you change a value in column B. The spreadsheet recalculates automatically. A dynamic table is the same idea, but for millions of database rows.
   163|
   164|Here is a simplified example:
   165|
   166|```sql
   167|-- This is NOT a view (which re-runs every time you query it).
   168|-- This is NOT a materialized view (which has restrictions on what SQL you can use).
   169|-- This is a DYNAMIC TABLE: Snowflake stores the result AND keeps it fresh.
   170|
   171|CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE DT_SIGNALS_FAST
   172|    TARGET_LAG = '5 minutes'        -- "keep this no more than 5 minutes stale"
   173|    WAREHOUSE = RC_PIPELINE_WH      -- "use this warehouse to refresh"
   174|    REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL      -- "only process what changed, not everything"
   175|AS
   176|SELECT
   177|    party_id,
   178|    COUNT(DISTINCT account_id) AS accounts_used,
   179|    SUM(amount) AS total_deposited,
   180|    ARRAY_AGG(txn_id) AS evidence_txn_ids
   181|FROM transactions_enriched
   182|WHERE is_cash = TRUE
   183|  AND amount BETWEEN 900000 AND 999900      -- structuring band
   184|GROUP BY party_id, time_window
   185|HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT account_id) >= 2;     -- 2+ accounts = suspicious
   186|```
   187|
   188|After this runs, `DT_SIGNALS_FAST` is a table you can SELECT from like any other table. But unlike a regular table, **you never INSERT into it**. Snowflake populates it by running the query, and re-runs it every 5 minutes (or sooner if something downstream needs it).
   189|
   190|### The dynamic tables in this project
   191|
   192|We have 5 dynamic tables, each one transforming data for the next:
   193|
   194|```
   195|RAW.RAW_PARTY + RAW.RAW_ACCOUNT
   196|    |
   197|    v
   198|DT_DIM_PARTY
   199|    What it does:  Joins party + account + KYC into one row per party
   200|    Why we need it: The agent needs "Rajesh Kumar, PAN ABCPK1234F, branch Delhi"
   201|                    in one query, not scattered across 3 raw tables
   202|    Refreshes:     On demand (only when something reads it)
   203|    Row count:     ~2,851 parties
   204|
   205|
   206|RAW.RAW_AMLWORLD_TRANS + DT_DIM_PARTY
   207|    |
   208|    v
   209|DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED
   210|    What it does:  Joins each transaction with its party names, account types,
   211|                   currency rates, and flags (is_cash, is_cross_border, is_internal)
   212|    Why we need it: Raw transactions don't have party names or cash flags.
   213|                    Every downstream table needs these enriched fields.
   214|    Refreshes:     Every 1 minute
   215|    Row count:     ~5 million enriched legs
   216|
   217|
   218|DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED
   219|    |
   220|    v
   221|DT_TXN_DAILY_AGG
   222|    What it does:  Summarizes each party's activity per day: total credits,
   223|                   total debits, cash amount, distinct counterparties
   224|    Why we need it: Rolling window features (7-day, 30-day) are built from
   225|                    daily buckets, not from scanning every individual transaction
   226|    Refreshes:     Every 5 minutes
   227|    Row count:     ~50,000 party-day rows
   228|
   229|
   230|DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED + GOVERNANCE.V_POLICY_CLAUSE_CURRENT
   231|    |
   232|    v
   233|DT_SIGNALS_FAST
   234|    What it does:  THE DETECTION ENGINE. Runs the structuring rule:
   235|                   finds parties with 2+ accounts receiving cash deposits
   236|                   between 90-99.9% of the CTR threshold within 7 days
   237|    Why we need it: This is where suspicion is born. Without this table,
   238|                    nobody knows which parties are structuring.
   239|    Refreshes:     Every 5 minutes
   240|    Row count:     10 signals (on the generated data)
   241|
   242|
   243|DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED
   244|    |
   245|    v
   246|DT_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP
   247|    What it does:  Computes fund flow edges and shared-device relationships
   248|                   from transaction patterns
   249|    Why we need it: Mule ring detection requires knowing who sends money to whom
   250|    Refreshes:     Every 60 minutes
   251|    Row count:     ~15,000 relationship edges
   252|```
   253|
   254|### Why dynamic tables instead of views or scheduled jobs
   255|
   256|| Approach | Problem |
   257||----------|---------|
   258|| Regular view | Re-runs the query every time you SELECT from it. On 5M rows, that's slow. The agent would wait minutes for each case lookup. |
   259|| Materialized view | Snowflake restricts what SQL you can put in a materialized view: no joins to other materialized views, limited aggregation. Our detection query is too complex. |
   260|| Scheduled stored procedure | You have to write the refresh logic yourself, handle failures, manage state. If the procedure crashes halfway, you have partial results. |
   261|| **Dynamic table** | Snowflake manages everything: scheduling, incremental refresh, failure retry, dependency ordering. You just write the query. The result is always fresh (within the target lag). |
   262|
   263|The `REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL` part is important. It means Snowflake doesn't re-scan all 5 million rows on every refresh. It only processes the rows that changed since the last refresh. On a system where new transactions arrive continuously, this keeps refresh times in seconds, not minutes.
   264|
   265|### How dynamic tables chain together
   266|
   267|Dynamic tables can read from other dynamic tables. Snowflake understands the dependency graph and refreshes them in the right order:
   268|
   269|```
   270|DT_DIM_PARTY (refreshes first, on demand)
   271|    |
   272|    v
   273|DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED (refreshes second, every 1 minute)
   274|    |
   275|    +---> DT_TXN_DAILY_AGG (refreshes third, every 5 minutes)
   276|    |
   277|    +---> DT_SIGNALS_FAST (refreshes third, every 5 minutes)
   278|    |
   279|    +---> DT_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP (refreshes third, every 60 minutes)
   280|```
   281|
   282|Snowflake guarantees: DT_SIGNALS_FAST will never refresh before DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED has finished its refresh. The data is always consistent across the chain.
   283|
   284|The project's config system (`conf/base.yml`) validates this dependency graph at load time. If you accidentally set DT_DIM_PARTY's lag to 1 day but DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED's lag to 1 minute, the config loader refuses to start — because Snowflake would reject a table whose lag is shorter than its upstream's lag.

   288|## 7. How the STR Agent Uses Dynamic Tables (The Connection)
   289|
   290|This is the part that connects everything together. Let's trace a concrete example.
   291|
   292|### The scenario
   293|
   294|Party `P-000000000042` (Rajesh Kumar) made three cash deposits:
   295|- Rs 9,50,000 on Sept 5 into account A-000000042
   296|- Rs 9,80,000 on Sept 7 into account A-000000101
   297|- Rs 9,70,000 on Sept 9 into account A-000000101
   298|
   299|All three are between 90-99.9% of Rs 10 lakh (the CTR threshold). Two different accounts were used within 7 days. This is textbook structuring.
   300|
   301|### Step 1: DT_SIGNALS_FAST detects it
   302|
   303|When the dynamic table refreshes, the structuring rule finds these three transactions. It produces one signal row:
   304|
   305|```
   306|rule_id:              STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT
   307|party_id:             P-000000000042
   308|metric_value:         2                    (2 distinct accounts)
   309|threshold_value:      2                    (minimum from POLICY_CLAUSE)
   310|evidence_txn_ids:     [TXN-00000001, TXN-00000002, TXN-00000003]
   311|signal_business_key:  STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT|P-000000000042|2022-09-05
   312|```
   313|
   314|**Notice `evidence_txn_ids`** — the signal carries the exact transaction IDs that caused it. This is how the agent will later find the actual amounts and dates.
   315|
   316|### Step 2: The router persists and deduplicates
   317|
   318|ROUTE_SIGNALS reads this signal from the stream and MERGEs it into the SIGNAL table. It also creates a CASE_RECORD for this party and a CASE_SIGNAL link.
   319|
   320|After routing:
   321|```
   322|SIGNAL:       signal_id = SIG-a1b2c3d4e5f6a1b2
   323|              (the SHA-256 hash of the business key)
   324|CASE_RECORD:  case_id = CASE-4399c4c86db5c6ea
   325|              party_id = P-000000000042
   326|              case_type = AML
   327|              branch_region = DELHI
   328|CASE_SIGNAL:  links the signal to the case
   329|```
   330|
   331|### Step 3: Analyst asks the agent
   332|
   333|The analyst types: "Generate STR for case CASE-4399c4c86db5c6ea"
   334|
   335|### Step 4: The agent calls COLLECT_CASE_EVIDENCE
   336|
   337|This procedure reads from the dynamic tables:
   338|
   339|**Read 1: CASE_RECORD** (not a dynamic table, but populated by the router)
   340|```sql
   341|SELECT party_id, case_type, branch_region
   342|FROM EVIDENCE_CHAIN.CASE_RECORD
   343|WHERE case_id = 'CASE-4399c4c86db5c6ea';
   344|-- Returns: P-000000000042, AML, DELHI
   345|```
   346|
   347|**Read 2: SIGNAL via CASE_SIGNAL** (not a dynamic table)
   348|```sql
   349|SELECT s.rule_id, s.severity, s.evidence_txn_ids, s.metric_value, s.threshold_value
   350|FROM EVIDENCE_CHAIN.SIGNAL s
   351|JOIN EVIDENCE_CHAIN.CASE_SIGNAL cs ON cs.signal_id = s.signal_id
   352|WHERE cs.case_id = 'CASE-4399c4c86db5c6ea';
   353|-- Returns: STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT, HIGH, [TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-003], 2, 2
   354|```
   355|
   356|**Read 3: DT_DIM_PARTY** (DYNAMIC TABLE -- this is the connection)
   357|```sql
   358|SELECT full_name, party_type, tax_id, nationality, kyc_status, risk_rating, branch_region
   359|FROM CURATED.DT_DIM_PARTY
   360|WHERE party_id = 'P-000000000042';
   361|-- Returns: Rajesh Kumar, INDIVIDUAL, ABCPK1234F, IND, VERIFIED, LOW, DELHI
   362|```
   363|
   364|Without DT_DIM_PARTY, the agent would have to join RAW_PARTY + RAW_ACCOUNT + RAW_KYC manually. The dynamic table has already done that join and keeps it fresh.
   365|
   366|**Read 4: DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED** (DYNAMIC TABLE -- this is the connection)

   368|SELECT txn_id, txn_date, amount_inr, channel, debit_party_name, credit_party_name, is_cash
   369|FROM CURATED.DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED

   372|-- TXN-00000001 | 2022-09-05 | 950000 | NEFT | Cash Desk Delhi | Rajesh Kumar | true

   462|                       (refreshes: on demand, when something reads it)
   463|                            |
   464|RAW.RAW_AMLWORLD_TRANS -----+--> DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED
   465|                                 (joins each transaction leg with its party
   466|                                  and account, adds FX rates, flags cash/
   467|                                  cross-border, resolves internal accounts)
   468|                                 (refreshes: every 1 minute)
   469|                                      |
   470|                                      +--> DT_TXN_DAILY_AGG
   471|                                      |    (daily summary per party: total credits,
   472|                                      |     debits, cash amounts, distinct counterparties)
   473|                                      |    (refreshes: every 5 minutes)
   474|                                      |
   475|                                      +--> V_TXN_VELOCITY_FEATURES (view)
   476|                                      |    (rolling 7d/30d/90d windows computed
   477|                                      |     from the daily aggregates)
   478|                                      |
   479|                                      +--> DT_SIGNALS_FAST
   480|                                           (THE DETECTION ENGINE -- see below)
   481|                                           (refreshes: every 5 minutes)
   482|```
   483|
   484|### 3b. How DT_SIGNALS_FAST Detects Structuring
   485|
   486|`DT_SIGNALS_FAST` is the dynamic table that runs the actual detection rules. For the
   487|structuring rule (`STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT`), here is what happens on every refresh:
   488|
   489|1. It reads all cash credit legs from `DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED`
   490|2. It joins to `GOVERNANCE.V_POLICY_CLAUSE_CURRENT` to get the **live thresholds**:
   491|   - CTR threshold: Rs 10,00,000 (from PMLA Rule 3(1)(A))
   492|   - Structuring band: 90-99.9% of CTR threshold
   493|   - Minimum accounts: 2 distinct accounts
   494|   - Window: 7 days
   495|3. It filters to deposits between Rs 9,00,000 and Rs 9,99,900
   496|4. It groups by (party, 7-day window) and checks: did this party deposit into 2+ accounts?
   497|5. If yes: a signal row is emitted
   498|
   499|**The key point:** The thresholds (Rs 10 lakh, 90%, 2 accounts, 7 days) are NOT hardcoded
   500|in the SQL. They come from `GOVERNANCE.POLICY_CLAUSE`, which is seeded from
   501|`conf/detection.yml`. If the regulator changes the threshold, you change the YAML, redeploy
   502|the policy stage, and the next DT refresh picks it up. No code change.
   503|
   504|After the refresh, `DT_SIGNALS_FAST` contains 10 rows -- one signal per planted
   505|structuring host. Each signal carries:
   506|- `rule_id`: which rule fired (STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT)
   507|- `party_id`: which party triggered it
   508|- `metric_value`: how many accounts (the observed value)
   509|- `threshold_value`: the minimum required (from policy)
   510|- `evidence_txn_ids`: an ARRAY of the exact transaction IDs that caused it
   511|- `signal_business_key`: a unique key for deduplication
   512|
   513|### 3c. The Stream and Triggered Task (Routing)
   514|
   515|Dynamic tables recompute their full result on every refresh. Without deduplication, the same
   516|10 signals would be inserted into SIGNAL every 5 minutes, creating thousands of duplicate
   517|cases. This is solved by a three-part routing system:
   518|
   519|```
   520|DT_SIGNALS_FAST
   521|    |
   522|    | (Snowflake stream -- captures changes)
   523|    v
   524|SIGNALS_STREAM
   525|    |
   526|    | (when stream has data, task fires automatically)
   527|    v
   528|ROUTE_SIGNALS_TASK
   529|    |
   530|    | (calls the router procedure)
   531|    v
   532|ROUTE_SIGNALS(full_scan BOOLEAN)
   533|    |
   534|    | One transaction: all or nothing
   535|    |
   536|    +---> SIGNAL table        (MERGE on signal_business_key -- no duplicates)
   537|    +---> CASE_RECORD table   (one case per party that needs one)
   538|    +---> CASE_SIGNAL table   (links signals to their case)
   539|```
   540|
   541|The router runs in a single database transaction. If anything fails, everything rolls back
   542|and the stream is unconsumed -- the next run retries the same data.
   543|
   544|**After routing completes**, the EVIDENCE_CHAIN schema contains:
   545|- 10 SIGNAL rows (deduplicated -- running the router again adds 0 rows)
   546|- 10 CASE_RECORD rows (one per structuring host, case_type = 'AML')
   547|- 10 CASE_SIGNAL rows (linking each signal to its case)
   548|
   549|**This is where the pipeline hands off to the agent.** Everything up to here is fully
   550|automatic. The agent enters the picture when an analyst asks about a case.

   604|## 6. How the Agent Works Inside Snowflake
   605|
   606|### 5a. What IS a Snowflake Cortex Agent?
   607|
   608|A Cortex Agent is a Snowflake object, like a table or a view. You create it with SQL:
   609|
   610|```sql
   611|CREATE AGENT my_agent FROM SPECIFICATION $$ ... $$;
   612|```
   613|
   614|It is stored in a schema, has an owner, and can be granted to roles. Snowflake runs it on
   615|its own infrastructure. You do not deploy it to a server.
   616|
   617|The agent has three parts:
   618|
   619|1. **Instructions** -- A system prompt that tells the AI who it is and how to behave
   620|2. **Tools** -- Procedures and functions the AI can call (database operations)
   621|3. **Budget** -- Time and token limits per conversation turn
   622|
   623|When a user sends a message, Snowflake's orchestration model reads the instructions,
   624|looks at the available tools, and decides which tool to call. The tool runs a stored
   625|procedure on a warehouse. The procedure's result goes back to the orchestration model,
   626|which formulates the response.
   627|
   628|```
   629|User message: "Generate STR for case CASE-xxx"
   630|        |
   631|        v
   632|+-------------------+
   633|| Orchestration     |  (Snowflake's built-in model)
   634|| Model             |  Reads: instructions, tool descriptions
   635||                   |  Decides: "I should call collect_case_evidence first"
   636|+--------+----------+
   637|         |
   638|         | Tool call: collect_case_evidence(case_id='CASE-xxx')
   639|         v
   640|+-------------------+
   641|| Warehouse         |  RC_DEMO_WH runs the SQL
   642|| (XSMALL)          |  Reads: SIGNAL, CASE_RECORD, DT_DIM_PARTY,
   643||                   |         DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED, V_POLICY_CLAUSE_CURRENT
   644|+--------+----------+
   645|         |
   646|         | Returns: JSON with party, transactions, signals, clauses
   647|         v
   648|+-------------------+
   649|| Orchestration     |  Decides: "Now I should call generate_str with this JSON"
   650|| Model             |
   651|+--------+----------+
   652|         |
   653|         | Tool call: generate_str(input_json='{...}')
   654|         v
   655|+-------------------+
   656|| Warehouse         |  RC_DEMO_WH runs:
   657|| (XSMALL)          |  1. VALIDATE_STR_INPUTS (checks fields)
   658||                   |  2. INSERT INTO STR_INPUT (audit trail)
   659||                   |  3. CORTEX.COMPLETE('claude-sonnet-4', prompt)  <-- THE LLM CALL
   660||                   |  4. INSERT INTO STR_OUTPUT (stores the draft)
   661|+--------+----------+
   662|         |
   663|         | Returns: { status: SUCCESS, narrative: "...", str_output_id: "..." }
   664|         v
   665|+-------------------+
   666|| Orchestration     |  Formats the response for the user
   667|| Model             |  "Here is your STR draft: ..."
   668|+-------------------+
   669|         |
   670|         v
   671|User sees the STR draft
   672|```
   673|
   674|### 5b. Where Does the LLM Call Happen?
   675|
   676|The LLM call is `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE('claude-sonnet-4', prompt)`. This is a built-in
   677|Snowflake function. It:
   678|
   679|- Runs inside Snowflake's infrastructure (not an external API call you manage)
   680|- Is billed as Snowflake credits (not a separate OpenAI/Anthropic bill)
   681|- Does not send your data outside Snowflake's security boundary
   682|- Supports multiple model families (Claude, GPT, Llama, Mistral)
   683|
   684|The prompt sent to the LLM contains the assembled evidence (party name, transactions,
   685|amounts, policy clauses) and instructions to write a formal STR narrative. The LLM writes
   686|prose. It does NOT compute numbers -- all figures (amounts, thresholds, counts) come from
   687|the SQL queries that ran before the LLM call.

   691|## 8. Task-by-Task: What We Build and Why
   692|
   693|### Task 1: The Evidence Collector
   694|
   695|**What:** A stored procedure called `COLLECT_CASE_EVIDENCE(case_id VARCHAR)`
   696|
   697|**Why it exists:** Today, the analyst has to manually look up the case, find its signals,
   698|look up each transaction by ID, find the party's KYC data, and copy-paste it all into a
   699|JSON payload. This procedure does all of that automatically.
   700|
   701|**Where it fits in the architecture:**
   702|
   703|```
   704|                        THE BRIDGE
   705|                    +------------------+
   706|  Pipeline output   |  COLLECT_CASE_   |   Agent input
   707|  (already exists)  |  EVIDENCE        |   (ready for LLM)
   708|                    |                  |
   709|  CASE_RECORD ------+-> reads case     |
   710|  CASE_SIGNAL ------+-> finds signals  +-----> JSON payload
   711|  SIGNAL -----------+-> gets evidence  |       compatible with
   712|  DT_DIM_PARTY -----+-> gets KYC data  |       GENERATE_STR
   713|  DT_TRANSACTIONS --+-> gets txns      |
   714|  V_POLICY_CLAUSE --+-> gets rules     |
   715|                    +------------------+
   716|```
   717|
   718|**How it works:**
   719|
   720|1. Takes a `case_id` as input
   721|2. Looks up the case in `CASE_RECORD` -- gets `party_id`, `case_type`, `branch_region`
   722|3. Finds all signals via `CASE_SIGNAL` join `SIGNAL` -- gets `rule_id`, `severity`,
   723|   `evidence_txn_ids` (the array of transaction IDs that caused each signal)
   724|4. Reads the party from `DT_DIM_PARTY` -- gets name, PAN, nationality, KYC status
   725|5. Reads the actual transactions from `DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED` using the evidence
   726|   transaction IDs -- gets dates, amounts, channels, counterparties
   727|6. Reads the policy clauses from `V_POLICY_CLAUSE_CURRENT` -- gets the regulatory
   728|   references (PMLA Rule 3(1)(A), etc.)
   729|7. Inserts EVIDENCE pointer rows (not copies -- just references with timestamps)
   730|8. Returns everything as a single JSON object
   731|
   732|**How it connects to the generated data:** The transaction IDs in `evidence_txn_ids`
   733|were assigned during `riskcopilot generate` and loaded during `riskcopilot load`. They
   734|trace all the way back to specific AMLworld pairs. When the evidence collector reads
   735|transaction TXN-xxx from `DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED`, that row contains the amount,
   736|channel, and parties that were generated from the source data.
   737|
   738|### Task 2: The STR Generator (already exists, gets enhanced)
   739|
   740|**What:** A stored procedure called `GENERATE_STR(input_json VARCHAR)`
   741|
   742|**Why it exists:** Takes the assembled evidence JSON and produces a formal STR narrative
   743|using an LLM. This procedure already exists in `sql/agents/str_generator_agent.sql`.
   744|
   745|**Enhancement:** Currently it only accepts raw JSON that the user assembles manually.
   746|We add the ability to accept a `case_id` and call `COLLECT_CASE_EVIDENCE` internally,
   747|so the user can say "generate STR for case X" without assembling any JSON.
   748|
   749|**How it works:**
   750|
   751|```
   752|Input JSON
   753|    |
   754|    v
   755|1. PARSE_JSON + VALIDATE_STR_INPUTS
   756|   (rejects if subject_name, suspicion_codes,
   757|    suspicion_summary, transactions, or accounts
   758|    are missing)
   759|    |
   760|    v
   761|2. INSERT INTO STR_INPUT
   762|   (audit trail -- every request is recorded)
   763|    |
   764|    v
   765|3. Build the prompt:
   766|   "You are a compliance officer generating an STR
   767|    for FIU-IND under PMLA 2002. Sections: Report
   768|    Details, Subject Info, Accounts, Transactions,
   769|    Related Parties, Grounds of Suspicion, Policy
   770|    Citations, Recommendation. Use ONLY the data
   771|    provided. Do NOT invent facts."
   772|   + the evidence JSON
   773|    |
   774|    v
   775|4. SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE('claude-sonnet-4', prompt)
   776|   (the actual LLM call -- runs inside Snowflake)
   777|    |
   778|    v
   779|5. INSERT INTO STR_OUTPUT
   780|   (stores the narrative + metadata)
   781|    |
   782|    v
   783|6. RETURN { status, narrative, str_output_id, next_steps }
   784|```
   785|
   786|**Why the numbers in the STR are trustworthy:** The prompt receives concrete numbers
   787|(Rs 9,50,000, Rs 9,80,000) that came from SQL queries against the actual transaction
   788|table. The LLM writes prose around those numbers but cannot change them. The STR_INPUT
   789|record preserves exactly what the LLM was shown. If anyone later asks "where did the
   790|Rs 9,50,000 figure come from?", the answer is traceable: STR_INPUT -> evidence_txn_ids
   791|-> DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED -> RAW.RAW_AMLWORLD_TRANS -> the generated Parquet file.

   793|### Task 3: The Adversarial Reviewer
   794|
   795|**What:** A stored procedure called `REVIEW_FINDING(finding_id VARCHAR)`
   796|
   797|**Why it exists:** An LLM-drafted narrative might contain errors: citing a transaction
   798|that doesn't exist, naming a policy clause that was not in force on the transaction
   799|date, or stating a number that doesn't match the database. The reviewer catches these
   800|before the MLRO sees the draft.
   801|
   802|**Where it fits:**
   803|
   804|```
   805|GENERATE_STR produces a FINDING row
   806|    |
   807|    v
   808|REVIEW_FINDING checks it
   809|    |
   810|    +---> Deterministic checks (SQL, not LLM):
   811|    |     - Every cited_evidence_id resolves to an EVIDENCE row?
   812|    |     - Every cited_clause_id is in force on the txn date?
   813|    |     - Every number in computed_values matches a re-run of the query?
   814|    |
   815|    +---> LLM check (DIFFERENT model family):
   816|    |     - Is the narrative internally consistent?
   817|    |     - Does it omit material evidence?
   818|    |     - Is the conclusion supported by the cited evidence?
   819|    |
   820|    v
   821|Writes a REVIEW row: APPROVE or REJECT with specific defects
   822|```
   823|
   824|**Why a different model family:** The STR narrative is drafted by an Anthropic model
   825|(Claude Sonnet). The reviewer is deliberately from a different family (OpenAI GPT or
   826|Meta Llama). This is defined in `conf/models.yml`:
   827|
   828|```
   829|drafter:   [claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-sonnet-4-6]   # Anthropic only
   830|reviewer:  [openai-gpt-5.1, llama3.3-70b, llama3.1-70b]         # Never Anthropic
   831|```
   832|
   833|A critic that shares the writer's training data and blind spots is not a useful critic.
   834|By using a different model family, we get genuinely independent verification.
   835|
   836|### Task 4: The Attestation Router
   837|
   838|**What:** A stored procedure called `REQUEST_ATTESTATION(finding_id VARCHAR)`
   839|
   840|**Why it exists:** After the reviewer approves a finding, the draft needs to be packaged
   841|as a formal artifact and routed to the MLRO for sign-off.
   842|
   843|**How it works:**
   844|
   845|1. Verifies the finding has a passing REVIEW (decision = 'APPROVE')
   846|2. Assembles the STR content from FINDING + EVIDENCE
   847|3. Computes a SHA-256 hash of the content
   848|4. Creates an ARTIFACT row with status = 'DRAFT' and the content hash
   849|5. Returns the artifact_id and instructions for the MLRO
   850|
   851|**What it does NOT do:** It does not insert into ATTESTATION. That table can only be
   852|written to by the `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER` role. The agent runs as `RC_SERVICE_ROLE`, which
   853|does not have INSERT privilege on ATTESTATION. This is the structural human gate --
   854|enforced by database privileges, not by a prompt instruction.
   855|
   856|```
   857|          CAN the agent do this?       WHO does it?
   858|          -------------------------    ----------------
   859|Step 1    Collect evidence             Agent (RC_SERVICE_ROLE)
   860|Step 2    Draft STR narrative          Agent (RC_SERVICE_ROLE)
   861|Step 3    Adversarial review           Agent (RC_SERVICE_ROLE)
   862|Step 4    Create artifact              Agent (RC_SERVICE_ROLE)
   863|Step 5    Sign off (attest)            HUMAN (COMPLIANCE_OFFICER role only)
   864|Step 6    File with FIU-IND            HUMAN (external system)
   865|```

     4|-- Human-gated state: the regulatory thresholds, the typology catalogue, the
     5|-- rule registry and the filing templates.
     6|--
     7|-- POLICY_CLAUSE is the runtime source of truth for every threshold. Detection
     8|-- SQL joins to it rather than embedding a literal, which is what turns
     9|-- "policy-as-data" from a slide into a property of the system: changing the CTR
    10|-- threshold is a governed, effective-dated data change with an audit trail,
    11|-- not a code deploy.

    14|USE SCHEMA {{ fq.governance }};

    16|-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    17|-- Effective-dated regulatory and internal thresholds.
    18|--
    19|-- Seeded from conf/detection.yml, which carries the provenance that the deploy
    20|-- gate requires: a clause with no source_document is rejected, which is how the
    21|-- demo is prevented from citing a circular number that does not exist.
    22|-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    23|CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS POLICY_CLAUSE (
    24|    clause_id               VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    25|    clause_version          NUMBER(10,0) NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    26|    source_document         VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'Real regulation or named internal document. Never blank.',

    54|FROM POLICY_CLAUSE
    55|QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY clause_id ORDER BY clause_version DESC) = 1

1|-- ===========================================================================
     2|-- 01_ddl / 01_raw_landing.sql
     3|-- ===========================================================================
     4|-- Immutable landing tables. Append-only: nothing here is ever updated in place,
     5|-- which is what makes Time Travel re-verification meaningful.
     6|--
     7|-- GAP-03 RESOLVED.  The architecture doc defined RAW_TRANSACTIONS twice --
     8|-- once pair-level and AMLworld-shaped (from_bank, amount_paid, is_laundering)
     9|-- and once leg-level with signed INR amounts. Both cannot hold. The split is
    10|-- explicit here:
    11|--
    12|--   RAW_AMLWORLD_TRANS   verbatim source, pair-level, label included
    13|--        |  reskin (FX -> INR, channel remap, pair -> two legs)
    14|--        +-> RAW_TRANSACTIONS            leg-level, signed INR, NO label
    15|--        +-> GROUND_TRUTH.TXN_LABELS     labels, isolated schema
    16|--
    17|-- Keeping the label out of RAW_TRANSACTIONS is not tidiness: RAW_TRANSACTIONS
    18|-- feeds the dynamic tables that feed the semantic view, so a label column here
    19|-- would leak the answer to the agent.
    20|-- ===========================================================================
    21|
    22|USE SCHEMA {{ fq.raw }};
    23|
    24|-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    25|-- Verbatim AMLworld landing (pair-level).
    26|--
    27|-- Loaded positionally ($1..$11) because columns 3 and 5 of HI-Small_Trans.csv
    28|-- share the header "Account"; a header-based load either errors or silently
    29|-- drops one of them.
    30|-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    31|CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS RAW_AMLWORLD_TRANS (
    32|    src_row_number      NUMBER(38,0)    NOT NULL COMMENT '1-based data-row ordinal: METADATA$FILE_ROW_NUMBER under SKIP_HEADER = 1, which does not count the header (M16). Joins GROUND_TRUTH.TXN_LABELS.src_row_number.',
    33|    txn_timestamp       TIMESTAMP_NTZ   NOT NULL COMMENT 'Source format YYYY/MM/DD HH:MI.',
    34|    from_bank           VARCHAR         NOT NULL,
    35|    from_account        VARCHAR         NOT NULL COMMENT 'CSV column 3 (hex). Unique only within from_bank.',
    36|    to_bank             VARCHAR         NOT NULL,
    37|    to_account          VARCHAR         NOT NULL COMMENT 'CSV column 5 (hex). Unique only within to_bank.',
    38|    amount_received     NUMBER(20,6)    NOT NULL COMMENT 'Credited to the beneficiary, in receiving_currency. Scale 6: Bitcoin carries 6 dp, every other currency 2 (M14); scale 2 would round a verbatim table.',
    39|    receiving_currency  VARCHAR         NOT NULL,
    40|    amount_paid         NUMBER(20,6)    NOT NULL COMMENT 'Debited from the originator, in payment_currency. Scale 6, as amount_received.',
    41|    payment_currency    VARCHAR         NOT NULL,
    42|    payment_format      VARCHAR         NOT NULL COMMENT 'ACH | Wire | Cheque | Cash | Credit Card | Reinvestment.',
    43|    is_laundering       NUMBER(1,0)     NOT NULL COMMENT 'Source ground truth. Routed to GROUND_TRUTH; never propagated to CURATED.',
    44|    loaded_at           TIMESTAMP_NTZ   DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() NOT NULL
    45|)
    46|COMMENT = 'IBM AMLworld HI-Small transactions, unmodified. Pair-level grain. CDLA-Sharing-1.0.';
    47|
    48|CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS RAW_AMLWORLD_ACCOUNTS (
    49|    bank_name       VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    50|    bank_id         VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    51|    account_number  VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'Hex. Unique only within bank_id -- see ids.account_id().',
    52|    entity_id       VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'Hex owning entity. The referential backbone (GAP-02).',
    53|    entity_name     VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'e.g. "Corporation #33520". party_type is derived from the prefix.',
    54|    loaded_at       TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() NOT NULL
    55|)
    56|COMMENT = 'AMLworld account-to-entity mapping. 518,581 rows. Source of the account/party skeleton.';
    57|
    58|-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    59|-- GAP-02: the identity maps.
    60|--
    61|-- These are the single most load-bearing tables in the build. The original plan
    62|-- generated Faker parties with fresh ids while transactions referenced AMLworld
    63|-- hex accounts, so every downstream join would have returned nothing. Instead,
    64|-- AMLworld keys are authoritative and the surrogate id is a deterministic
    65|-- function of the source key (risk_copilot.ids). Referential integrity then
    66|-- holds by construction rather than by convention.
    67|-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    68|CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ID_MAP_PARTY (
    69|    party_id        VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'Surrogate P-####### from ids.party_id(entity_id, seed).',
    70|    src_entity_id   VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'AMLworld entity_id (hex).',
    71|    generation_seed NUMBER(38,0) NOT NULL COMMENT 'Seed that produced this mapping. Reproducibility anchor.',
    72|    in_subgraph     BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE COMMENT 'Survived subgraph sampling.',
    73|    loaded_at       TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() NOT NULL,
    74|    CONSTRAINT pk_id_map_party PRIMARY KEY (party_id),
    75|    CONSTRAINT uk_id_map_party_src UNIQUE (src_entity_id)
    76|)
    77|COMMENT = 'Deterministic AMLworld entity_id -> party_id map. Asserted 1:1 at generation time.';
    78|
    79|CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ID_MAP_ACCOUNT (
    80|    account_id          VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'Surrogate A-######## from ids.account_id(bank_id, account_number, seed).',
    81|    src_bank_id         VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    82|    src_account_number  VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    83|    party_id            VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'Owning party. FK to ID_MAP_PARTY.',
    84|    generation_seed     NUMBER(38,0) NOT NULL,
    85|    in_subgraph         BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
    86|    loaded_at           TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() NOT NULL,
    87|    CONSTRAINT pk_id_map_account PRIMARY KEY (account_id),
    88|    CONSTRAINT uk_id_map_account_src UNIQUE (src_bank_id, src_account_number),
    89|    CONSTRAINT fk_id_map_account_party FOREIGN KEY (party_id) REFERENCES ID_MAP_PARTY (party_id)
    90|)
    91|COMMENT = 'Deterministic (bank_id, account_number) -> account_id map. Composite key is required: AMLworld account numbers repeat across banks, and deriving from the number alone would merge distinct accounts and corrupt the counterparty graph.';
    92|
    93|-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------
    94|-- Leg-level transactions -- the table the pipeline actually reads.
    95|--
    96|-- One AMLworld pair row becomes two rows sharing txn_pair_id: a signed-negative
    97|-- debit and a signed-positive credit. Signed amounts make inflow and outflow a
    98|-- filter rather than a column, which keeps the velocity SQL simple.
    99|--
   100|-- Deliberately NOT present: is_laundering. See the header note.
   101|-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------
   102|CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS RAW_TRANSACTIONS (
   103|    txn_id                  VARCHAR         NOT NULL COMMENT 'T-############-D|C.',
   104|    txn_pair_id             VARCHAR         NOT NULL COMMENT 'Links the two legs of one transfer (GAP-03).',
   105|    leg_side                VARCHAR(1)      NOT NULL COMMENT 'D = debit (negative), C = credit (positive).',
   106|    account_id              VARCHAR         NOT NULL COMMENT 'The account this leg posts to.',
   107|    counterparty_account_id VARCHAR         NOT NULL COMMENT 'The other side. Resolvable by construction.',
   108|    txn_timestamp           TIMESTAMP_NTZ   NOT NULL,
   109|    amount                  NUMBER(20,2)    NOT NULL COMMENT 'Signed, in `currency`. Negative = debit.',
   110|    currency                VARCHAR         NOT NULL COMMENT 'INR for ~95% of legs; the rest cross-border.',
   111|    amount_inr              NUMBER(20,2)    NOT NULL COMMENT 'Converted at the per-currency rate in conf/generation.yml. All threshold arithmetic uses this column.',
   112|    txn_type                VARCHAR         NOT NULL COMMENT 'DEPOSIT | WITHDRAWAL | TRANSFER | PAYMENT.',
   113|    channel                 VARCHAR         NOT NULL COMMENT 'UPI | IMPS | NEFT | RTGS | CASH | CHEQUE.',
   114|    reference_text          VARCHAR         COMMENT 'Free-text narration. Synthetic.',
   115|    source_ref              VARCHAR         COMMENT 'Opaque UTR-like transfer reference, shared by both legs. Deliberately carries no provenance: a source/injected prefix or a source row number would be a label. Provenance is in GROUND_TRUTH.TXN_LABELS.',
   116|    ingested_at             TIMESTAMP_NTZ   DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() NOT NULL
   117|                                            COMMENT 'Arrival time. Differs from txn_timestamp under replay.',
   118|    CONSTRAINT pk_raw_transactions PRIMARY KEY (txn_id),
   119|    CONSTRAINT fk_raw_txn_account FOREIGN KEY (account_id) REFERENCES ID_MAP_ACCOUNT (account_id)
   120|)
   121|CLUSTER BY (TO_DATE(txn_timestamp), account_id)
   122|COMMENT = 'Leg-level transaction ledger, INR-normalised. Append-only. Contains NO label column: it feeds the dynamic tables that feed the semantic view.';

   124|-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------

   127|-- A real institution holds the same customer in a core banking system and a KYC
   128|-- platform, and they disagree. Modelling that disagreement is the point: the
   129|-- L3 generator injects contradictions at a configured rate, and DT_DIM_PARTY
   130|-- has to resolve them.

   140|    branch_code         VARCHAR NOT NULL,
   141|    customer_since      DATE,
   142|    status              VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'ACTIVE | DORMANT | CLOSED.',
   143|    loaded_at           TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() NOT NULL,
   144|    CONSTRAINT pk_raw_party_cbs PRIMARY KEY (party_id)
   145|)
   146|COMMENT = 'Core banking system view of the customer. System of record for identity and branch.';
   147|
   148|CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS RAW_PARTY_KYC (
   149|    party_id                VARCHAR NOT NULL,
   150|    occupation              VARCHAR         COMMENT 'Deliberately stale for a configured share of parties.',
   151|    declared_annual_income  NUMBER(20,2)    COMMENT 'GAP-04: derived from observed legitimate inflow, not drawn at random, or INCOME_ACTIVITY_MISMATCH fires on everyone or no one.',
   152|    source_of_funds         VARCHAR,

   156|    kyc_last_reviewed       DATE,

   158|    aadhaar_last4           VARCHAR         COMMENT 'Synthetic. Masked for non-privileged roles.',
   159|    phone_number            VARCHAR         COMMENT 'Shared across parties by design -> SHARED_PHONE edges.',
   160|    kyc_note                VARCHAR         COMMENT 'L3 narrative. May contradict the structured record.',
   161|    loaded_at               TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() NOT NULL,
   162|    CONSTRAINT pk_raw_party_kyc PRIMARY KEY (party_id),
   163|    CONSTRAINT fk_raw_party_kyc_party FOREIGN KEY (party_id) REFERENCES RAW_PARTY_CBS (party_id)
   164|)
   165|COMMENT = 'KYC/CDD platform view. Source for income, PEP status and narrative notes.';
   166|
   167|CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS RAW_ACCOUNTS (
   168|    account_id          VARCHAR NOT NULL,
   169|    party_id            VARCHAR NOT NULL,
   170|    account_type        VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'SAVINGS | CURRENT | LOAN | CREDIT_CARD | FD.',
   171|    opened_date         DATE    NOT NULL,
   172|    status              VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'ACTIVE | DORMANT | FROZEN | CLOSED.',
   173|    current_balance     NUMBER(20,2),
   174|    credit_limit        NUMBER(20,2)    COMMENT 'NULL unless a credit product.',
   175|    branch_region       VARCHAR NOT NULL COMMENT 'Denormalised from the party for row-level filtering.',
   176|    branch_code         VARCHAR NOT NULL,
   177|    device_fingerprint  VARCHAR         COMMENT 'GAP-05: shared fingerprints are co-located with existing fund flows. Random assignment yields zero SHARED_DEVICE_CLUSTER hits, because that rule requires a shared device AND a flow between the accounts.',
   178|    loaded_at           TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() NOT NULL,
   179|    CONSTRAINT pk_raw_accounts PRIMARY KEY (account_id),
   180|    CONSTRAINT fk_raw_accounts_party FOREIGN KEY (party_id) REFERENCES RAW_PARTY_CBS (party_id)
   181|)

  1073|
  1074|## 10. Cloud Architecture -- Why No External Hosting
  1075|
  1076|### The traditional way (what you DON'T need to do):
  1077|
  1078|```
  1079|                     THE HARD WAY
  1080|  Snowflake ----API----> Your server ----API----> OpenAI
  1081|  (data)                (Node.js/Python)          (LLM)
  1082|                        on Vercel/AWS/GCP
  1083|                        
  1084|  Problems:
  1085|  - Transaction data leaves Snowflake
  1086|  - You manage API keys for OpenAI
  1087|  - You manage hosting, scaling, monitoring
  1088|  - You manage auth between all three systems
  1089|  - Data transfer costs
  1090|  - Latency from network hops
  1091|```
  1092|
  1093|### The Snowflake way (what we do):
  1094|
  1095|```
  1096|                     THE SIMPLE WAY
  1097|  +-------------------------------------------+
  1098|  |            SNOWFLAKE ACCOUNT               |
  1099|  |                                            |
  1100|  |  Data (tables) ---> Agent (procedures)     |
  1101|  |                       |                    |
  1102|  |                       v                    |
  1103|  |               CORTEX.COMPLETE              |
  1104|  |               (built-in LLM)               |
  1105|  |                       |                    |
  1106|  |                       v                    |
  1107|  |               Response (JSON)              |
  1108|  |                                            |
  1109|  +-------------------------------------------+
  1110|         |
  1111|         | SQL API (built-in REST endpoint)
  1112|         v
  1113|  Any HTTP client (Postman, curl, React app, mobile app)
  1114|```
  1115|
  1116|**Everything runs inside Snowflake:**
  1117|- Data never leaves the account
  1118|- LLM calls are a built-in function, not an external API
  1119|- The agent is a database object, not a running server
  1120|- The REST endpoint is Snowflake's SQL API, not something you deploy
  1121|- Auth is Snowflake auth (OAuth, key-pair, password -- whatever you already use)
  1122|- Scaling is automatic (warehouse auto-resume, auto-suspend)
  1123|
  1124|**To "deploy to the cloud":** Run `riskcopilot deploy --profile dev`. That's it.
  1125|Snowflake IS the cloud.
  1126|
  1127|**To get a REST endpoint:** Use Snowflake's SQL API:
  1128|
  1129|```
  1130|POST https://<account>.snowflakecomputing.com/api/v2/statements
  1131|```
  1132|
  1133|This endpoint already exists for every Snowflake account. You don't create it. You
  1134|don't deploy it. You just send SQL to it, and the SQL calls the agent.
  1135|
  1136|---
  1137|
  1138|## 11. Security and the Human Gate
  1139|
  1140|### Role-Based Access Control
  1141|
  1142|```
  1143|                    ACCOUNTADMIN
  1144|                         |
  1145|                    RC_ADMIN (owns all objects)
  1146|                    /         \
  1147|        RC_SERVICE_ROLE    COMPLIANCE_OFFICER
  1148|        (agent runs as)    (human reviewers)
  1149|              |                    |
  1150|              |              BRANCH_ANALYST_MUMBAI
  1151|              |              BRANCH_ANALYST_DELHI
  1152|              |              (filtered by row access policy)
  1153|              |
  1154|        Can do:              Cannot do:
  1155|        - Read all data      - Write ATTESTATION
  1156|        - Run agent          - Read GROUND_TRUTH
  1157|        - Write SIGNAL       - File with FIU-IND
  1158|        - Write CASE         - Change ARTIFACT to FILED
  1159|        - Write STR_INPUT
  1160|        - Write STR_OUTPUT
  1161|        - Write EVIDENCE
  1162|        - Write FINDING
  1163|        - Write REVIEW
  1164|        - Write ARTIFACT
  1165|```
  1166|
  1167|### The Attestation Gate (Why the Agent Cannot File)
  1168|
  1169|Under PMLA Rule 7, the Principal Officer must personally attest before filing. This is
  1170|enforced by database privileges:
  1171|
  1172|```
  1173|ATTESTATION table
  1174|    |
  1175|    | INSERT privilege granted ONLY to COMPLIANCE_OFFICER
  1176|    | RC_SERVICE_ROLE (agent) does NOT have INSERT
  1177|    |
  1178|    | content_hash column: SHA-256 of the artifact content
  1179|    |   - If someone edits the STR after sign-off, the hash won't match
  1180|    |   - The filing procedure checks: artifact.content_hash = attestation.attested_content_hash
  1181|    |   - A mismatch blocks the filing
  1182|    |
  1183|    | No ARTIFACT can reach status FILED without a matching ATTESTATION row
  1184|```
  1185|
  1186|This cannot be bypassed by prompt injection, jailbreaking, or any other AI attack.
  1187|It is a missing database privilege. The agent's role literally cannot execute the
  1188|INSERT statement.
  1189|
  1190|### Ground Truth Isolation
  1191|
  1192|The generated data includes labels: which parties are actually laundering. These labels
  1193|are in `GROUND_TRUTH.GROUND_TRUTH_STAGE`, and no role (not even COMPLIANCE_OFFICER)
  1194|can read them. This means:
  1195|
  1196|- The agent cannot cheat by looking at the answer key
  1197|- Dynamic tables cannot use labels as detection features
  1198|- The detection system proves its value honestly
  1199|
  1200|---
  1201|
  1202|## 12. One-Command Deploy
  1203|
  1204|### The deploy pipeline
  1205|
  1206|The existing deployer (`src/risk_copilot/pipeline/deploy.py`) processes SQL stages
  1207|in a fixed order:
  1208|
  1209|```
  1210|riskcopilot deploy --profile dev
  1211|
  1212|Stage 0:  bootstrap        sql/00_bootstrap/       Database, schemas, warehouses, roles
  1213|Stage 1:  ddl              sql/01_ddl/             28+ tables across 7 schemas
  1214|Stage 2:  dynamic_tables   sql/02_dynamic_tables/  8 dynamic tables + 2 views
  1215|Stage 3:  streams_tasks    sql/03_streams_tasks/   Stream, router, triggered task
  1216|Stage 4:  governance       sql/04_governance/      Row access policies, masking
  1217|Stage 5:  policy           sql/05_policy/          Seeds POLICY_CLAUSE from YAML
  1218|Stage 6:  search           sql/06_search/          Cortex Search service
  1219|Stage 7:  semantic         sql/07_semantic/         Semantic View
  1220|Stage 8:  agent            sql/08_agent/           <<< THE AGENT LIVES HERE >>>
  1221|Stage 9:  ml               sql/09_ml/              ML model registration
  1222|```
  1223|
  1224|Every SQL file is a Jinja template. The deployer substitutes values from
  1225|`conf/base.yml` + `conf/profiles/dev.yml`:
  1226|
  1227|```
  1228|{{ fq.evidence }}  --->  RISK_COPILOT.EVIDENCE_CHAIN
  1229|{{ wh.demo }}      --->  RC_DEMO_WH
  1230|{{ cortex.agent }} --->  RISK_COPILOT_AGENT_DEV
  1231|```
  1232|
  1233|This is what makes `--profile dev` and `--profile demo` coexist in one account: the
  1234|object names get different suffixes.
  1235|
  1236|### What stage 8 (agent) deploys
  1237|
  1238|```
  1239|sql/08_agent/
  1240|  01_str_tables.sql          STR_INPUT, STR_OUTPUT tables
  1241|  02_str_procedures.sql      VALIDATE_STR_INPUTS, GENERATE_STR
  1242|  03_evidence_collector.sql  COLLECT_CASE_EVIDENCE
  1243|  04_review.sql              REVIEW_FINDING
  1244|  05_attestation.sql         REQUEST_ATTESTATION
  1245|  06_agent.sql               CREATE AGENT with all tools
  1246|  07_grants.sql              Role grants for all objects
  1247|```
  1248|
  1249|Each file uses `CREATE OR REPLACE` or `IF NOT EXISTS`, so running the deploy again
  1250|is safe -- it overwrites procedures and recreates the agent with any updated
  1251|instructions or tools.
  1252|
  1253|### To deploy only the agent (after changes):
  1254|
  1255|```bash
  1256|riskcopilot deploy --profile dev --stage agent
  1257|```
  1258|
  1259|### To deploy everything from scratch:
  1260|
  1261|```bash
  1262|riskcopilot deploy --profile dev
  1263|```

  1267|## 13. Talking to the Agent
  1268|
  1269|Once deployed, there are four ways to interact with the agent. All of them ultimately
  1270|call the same function: `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.DATA_AGENT_RUN`.
  1271|
  1272|### Way 1: Snowsight (Browser UI)
  1273|
  1274|Open Snowsight > AI & ML > Agents > RISK_COPILOT_AGENT_DEV. Type in the chat box.
  1275|
  1276|### Way 2: SQL (Any SQL Client)
  1277|
  1278|```sql

  1280|    'RISK_COPILOT.EVIDENCE_CHAIN.RISK_COPILOT_AGENT_DEV',
  1281|    '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text",
  1282|      "text":"Generate STR for case CASE-4399c4c86db5c6ea"}]}]}',
  1283|    TRUE   -- TRUE = streaming response
  1284|) AS response;

  1339|## 14. Design Decision Log
  1340|
  1341|| ID | Decision | Why | Alternative Rejected |
  1342||----|----------|-----|---------------------|
  1343|| D1 | Everything runs inside Snowflake, no external hosting | Data never leaves; no infra to manage | Web app on Vercel/AWS -- adds complexity, security risk, cost |
  1344|| D2 | Thresholds live in POLICY_CLAUSE, not in code | Changing a threshold is a governed data change with audit trail, not a code deploy | Hardcoded values in SQL -- no audit trail, requires code review for a number change |
  1345|| D3 | Agent runs as RC_SERVICE_ROLE, not ACCOUNTADMIN | Principle of least privilege; cannot access GROUND_TRUTH or ATTESTATION | Running as admin -- too many privileges, no separation of duties |
  1346|| D4 | ATTESTATION requires COMPLIANCE_OFFICER role | PMLA Rule 7 legal requirement; structural enforcement, not prompt-based | Prompt instruction "don't file automatically" -- can be bypassed |
  1347|| D5 | Reviewer uses a different AI model family | Independent verification; different training data and blind spots | Same model reviews its own work -- confirmation bias |
  1348|| D6 | Evidence rows are pointers, not copies | Copied data diverges from the source over time; a pointer + as_of_ts stays true | Copy-on-read -- eventually inconsistent, harder to re-verify |
  1349|| D7 | Signal deduplication via MERGE on business_key | DTs recompute fully on every refresh; without MERGE, duplicates grow linearly | Delete-and-reinsert -- loses first_seen_at history, not atomic |
  1350|| D8 | Stream-triggered task, not scheduled polling | Runs within 30s of a real change; never wastes compute on empty polls | CRON schedule -- either too frequent (wasteful) or too slow |
  1351|| D9 | Numbers in STR come from SQL, narrative from LLM | "No number in a filing comes from a language model" -- the FINDING.computed_values mechanism | Let the LLM compute amounts -- unreliable, not auditable |
  1352|| D10 | Content hash binds attestation to exact artifact version | Post-attestation edits are caught mechanically | Trust-based: "nobody would edit after sign-off" -- unenforceable |
  1353|| D11 | Cortex Search for regulatory citations | Agent cites real PMLA sections, not hallucinated circular numbers | LLM generates citations from training data -- often wrong |
  1354|| D12 | One-command deploy via riskcopilot CLI | Reproducible, idempotent, profile-aware; no manual SQL execution | Run SQL files by hand in Snowsight -- error-prone, environment-specific |

    55|def _load_dotenv(start: Path | None = None) -> Path | None:
    56|    """Load ``.env`` into the environment, returning the file used.
    57|
    58|    ``.env`` holds pointers -- which connection to use, where the private key
    59|    lives -- and every consumer reads them via :mod:`os.environ`. Loading it
    60|    here means one entry point applies it, so a developer does not have to
    61|    export the same variables by hand in every shell. Values already present in
    62|    the environment win, so an explicit ``RC_*`` override on the command line is
    63|    never clobbered by the file. Parsed with the standard library rather than
    64|    adding a dependency for eight lines of work.
    65|    """
    66|    origin = (start or Path.cwd()).resolve()
    67|    for directory in (origin, *origin.parents):
    68|        candidate = directory / ".env"
    69|        if candidate.is_file():
    70|            break
    71|    else:
    72|        return None
    73|
    74|    for raw in candidate.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
    75|        line = raw.strip()
    76|        if not line or line.startswith("#") or "=" not in line:
    77|            continue
    78|        key, _, value = line.partition("=")
    79|        key = key.strip()
    80|        value = value.strip().strip('"').strip("'")
    81|        if key and key not in os.environ:
    82|            os.environ[key] = value
    83|    return candidate
